\chapter{Time --- Day, Night, and When Things Happen}
\label{ch:sa-time}
\hlchaptermodality{17}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the parts of a day in Sanskrit, say today, yesterday and always, and place a time word in a sentence.}

Complete SA-C17-time-words and demonstrate the chapter promise.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[dinam]{\sk{दिनम्} (dinam) — day}

\label{lesson:SA-C17-day}



\begin{quote}
You have places. Now you need times to put in them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{दिनम्}}
\textbf{\sk{दिनम्}} (\emph{dinam}) — \textquotedblleft{}day.\textquotedblright{}

It belongs to one of the oldest word-families in the language. The Indo-European root for the bright sky, \emph{*dyew-}, gave Sanskrit \textbf{\sk{द्यौः}} (\emph{dyauḥ}), the sky itself, and it is the same root standing behind Latin \emph{diēs}, \textquotedblleft{}day,\textquotedblright{} and the god names \emph{Iuppiter} and \emph{Zeus}. A day, to the people who coined the word, was simply \emph{the bright}.

Its ending is \emph{-am}, so you already know its family without being told: neuter, like \sk{गृहम्} and \sk{वनम्}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Your first time word, and it arrived with its family badge already legible. That is what the ending work bought you.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dinam} — \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}a good day\textquotedblright{} — \emph{uttama dinam}
  \item which family it belongs to, from the ending alone
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did the root behind \sk{दिनम्} originally mean? (The bright sky.) Which family does it belong to, and how do you know? (Neuter — the \emph{-am} ending.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rātriḥ]{\sk{रात्रिः} (rātriḥ) — night}

\label{lesson:SA-C17-night}



\begin{quote}
The other half of the day.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{रात्रिः}}
\textbf{\sk{रात्रिः}} (\emph{rātriḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}night.\textquotedblright{}

Where \sk{दिनम्} is the bright, \sk{रात्रिः} is its opposite, and the pair is one of the oldest ways any language divides the world. In the hymns it is a name as much as a noun: Rātrī is addressed directly, a presence rather than an absence of light.

The ending here is \emph{-iḥ}, which is neither of the two you have met. Sanskrit has more than two families, and this is your first sight of a third. You do not need it yet — only the honest note that the system is bigger than the part you have seen.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Day and night, and a quiet warning: the \emph{-am} / \emph{-aḥ} division you learned is real but not the whole map.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{rātriḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair together — \emph{dinam}, \emph{rātriḥ}
  \item which ending is new to you here
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \sk{रात्रिः} in the hymns, beyond a noun? (A presence addressed by name.) What does its ending tell you? (That there are more than two noun families.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[adya]{\sk{अद्य} (adya) — today}

\label{lesson:SA-C17-today}



\begin{quote}
Naming the day you are standing in.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{अद्य}}
\textbf{\sk{अद्य}} (\emph{adya}) — \textquotedblleft{}today.\textquotedblright{}

Take it apart and the older shape shows: \emph{a-} (\textquotedblleft{}this\textquotedblright{}) plus the same \emph{dy-} that sits inside \sk{दिनम्} and \sk{द्यौः}. \textbf{This day} — said so often that the two halves fused and stopped being separable for ordinary speakers.

This is how a great many everyday words are built, in Sanskrit and elsewhere. English \emph{today} is \emph{to} + \emph{day}, and \emph{tomorrow} is \emph{to} + \emph{morrow}: the same trick, a thousand years later, in a different family.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word you can now see through. When a short everyday word looks unanalysable, it is usually a fused phrase that got worn smooth.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{adya} — \textquotedblleft{}today\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two pieces inside it — \emph{a-} and \emph{dy-}
  \item the English word built the same way (\emph{today})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two pieces of \sk{अद्य}? (\emph{A-}, \textquotedblleft{}this,\textquotedblright{} and the \emph{dy-} of \textquotedblleft{}day.\textquotedblright{}) What English word is built the same way? (\emph{Today}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hyaḥ]{\sk{ह्यः} (hyaḥ) — yesterday}

\label{lesson:SA-C17-yesterday}



\begin{quote}
The day behind you — and a word with relatives you already speak.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{ह्यः}}
\textbf{\sk{ह्यः}} (\emph{hyaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}yesterday.\textquotedblright{}

This one is a gift, because its cousins are everywhere. The same ancestral word gave Latin \emph{heri}, which became Spanish \emph{ayer} and French \emph{hier}; and it gave Germanic \emph{gester-}, which is the \textbf{yester-} still sitting inside English \emph{yesterday}.

So \sk{ह्यः}, \emph{heri}, \emph{ayer} and \emph{yester-} are four survivals of one word for \textquotedblleft{}the day before this one,\textquotedblright{} spoken continuously for as long as any of these languages have existed. Very few words let you see that far back this clearly.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word that is genuinely easier to keep because of what it is related to. When a Sanskrit word has a visible European cousin, learn them as one thing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hyaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}yesterday\textquotedblright{}
  \item its Latin cousin — \emph{heri}
  \item the English word that still carries it (\emph{yester}day)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Latin word is \sk{ह्यः} related to? (\emph{Heri}.) What English word still carries the same root? (\emph{Yester}day.) What does the family all mean? (The day before this one.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sadā]{\sk{सदा} (sadā) — always}

\label{lesson:SA-C17-always}



\begin{quote}
Today, yesterday — and the word for every day there is.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{सदा}}
\textbf{\sk{सदा}} (\emph{sadā}) — \textquotedblleft{}always, ever.\textquotedblright{}

It carries the sense of \emph{sa-}, \textquotedblleft{}together, whole, the same\textquotedblright{} — the element behind Sanskrit \textbf{\sk{सम}} (\emph{sama}), \textquotedblleft{}same, equal,\textquotedblright{} and behind English \textbf{same} itself. Always is the whole of time taken at once.

Where the other four words in this chapter point at one particular time, \sk{सदा} refuses to. That is what makes it useful with the verbs you already have: \sk{सदा} \sk{पठति}, \textquotedblleft{}he reads always.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five time words: two nouns, three that simply attach to a verb and say when.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sadā} — \textquotedblleft{}always\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}he always reads\textquotedblright{} — \emph{sadā paṭhati}
  \item the English word related to its first piece (\emph{same})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the \emph{sa-} in \sk{सदा} carry? (Together, whole, the same.) Which English word shares it? (\emph{Same}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kāla-śabdāḥ]{\sk{कालशब्दाः} (kāla-śabdāḥ) — where a time word stands}

\label{lesson:SA-C17-time-words}



\begin{quote}
You have five time words. This is where they go.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{कालशब्दाः}}
Three of this chapter's words — \sk{अद्य}, \sk{ह्यः}, \sk{सदा} — are not nouns at all. Look for an \emph{-am} or \emph{-aḥ} or \emph{-iḥ} on them and you will not find one. They attach to a sentence, say \emph{when}, and keep the same shape wherever they land.

Sanskrit lets them stand almost anywhere. \sk{सदा} \sk{पठति} and \sk{पठति} \sk{सदा} both say \textquotedblleft{}he always reads,\textquotedblright{} and neither is more correct than the other. You have been given a lot of attention to endings, and this is the payoff: they are carrying the work that word order carries in English.

The two that \emph{are} nouns, \sk{दिनम्} and \sk{रात्रिः}, behave like any other noun, and take adjectives in front of them the way \sk{गृहम्} does.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now say when something happens, and you have met the single most important fact about Sanskrit word order: it is loose because the endings are strict.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}he always reads,\textquotedblright{} both ways round
  \item \textquotedblleft{}a good day\textquotedblright{} — \emph{uttama dinam}
  \item which three of the five never change
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which three words never change their ending? (\sk{अद्य}, \sk{ह्यः}, \sk{सदा}.) Why can Sanskrit move words around freely? (Because the endings carry the grammar, not the order.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṣa]{\sk{ष} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S118-letter-ssa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \sk{ठ} — what does it do?

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{ष}}
\textbf{\sk{ष}} — \emph{ṣa}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{ṣ}, it is \textbf{ṣa}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a U-shaped body drawn from the left side around the lower bowl and up the right side
  \item a retraced top-to-bottom right stem
  \item a down-right inner diagonal
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \sk{ष} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{क्षीरम्}} \emph{kṣīram} — milk
  \item \textbf{\sk{अक्षि}} \emph{akṣi} — eye
  \item \textbf{\sk{अक्षिणी}} \emph{akṣiṇī} — two eyes, the dual
\end{itemize}

In every one of those words \sk{ष} is riding inside a \textbf{conjunct}: \sk{क्} + \sk{ष} fused into the single shape \sk{क्ष}. Owning both halves is not owning the join — \sk{क्ष} has a look of its own and gets its own lesson later. For now: find the \sk{ष} in it, and let the rest wait.

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{ष}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} descend the left side, curve counterclockwise around the lower bowl, and rise along the right side to the headline without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom, retracing its upper body-side segment before continuing below the bowl
  \item \textbf{3.} lift at the upper-left interior and draw the inner diagonal down-right to the bowl junction
  \item \textbf{4.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 3.} The pen comes up 3 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
Verified four-stroke teaching form fitted to the bundled printed outline.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\sk{ष}-order.gif’, strokes 1–4, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \sk{ष} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{अक्षि}  ·  \sk{पठति}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{ष} three times, saying \emph{ṣa} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{ष} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{ष}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ṣa}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
